title: Recursion
summary: Recursion is a function solving a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of it. Every recursive function needs a base case (when to stop) and a step that shrinks the problem. The lesson compares recursion with while loops, explains the call stack, and rewrites binary search recursively. Step-by-step guide arrives when the lecture is published.
goal: Write a recursive function with a correct base case and trace how its calls stack up and return.

steps.title: Read the lesson
steps.detail: Read the Recursion page, focusing on 'Identifying the Stopping Condition' and 'The Call Stack'.
steps.doneWhen: You can point to the base case and the shrinking step in any recursive function.

steps.title: Run factorial both ways
steps.detail: Run the lesson's loop and recursive versions side by side, then try factorial(-1) on the recursive one to see what a missing base case does.
steps.doneWhen: Both print 120, and the negative input ends in a RecursionError.

steps.title: Watch the call stack in Python Tutor
steps.detail: One assignment asks you to step through a recursive function in Python Tutor. Paste factorial(3) there and step forward. Note: the lesson's recursive binary search calls binary_search2 inside binary_search, so rename it to one name if you try it.
steps.doneWhen: You saw three factorial frames stack up and then return 6.

steps.title: Talk through Flatten List first
steps.detail: Flatten List is one of the assignments. Before coding, say the base case (an item that isn't a list) and the recursive case (flatten each sub-list), then the Big-O: time O(n) over all items, space O(d) for nesting depth d.
steps.doneWhen: You can explain the approach and its Big-O out loud.

concepts.meaning: A function that calls itself on a smaller piece of the problem.
The condition where the function stops calling itself and returns a value.
The part that calls the function again with a smaller input.
Python's list of function calls still waiting to finish.
Python's error when the call stack gets too deep, usually from a missing base case.
